slides.heading: Year 1 — Autumn 1, Week 2
slides.sub: New content taught directly, practised in words/sentences and applied in reading and dictation.

slides.heading: Mon
slides.objective: Learn the new sound "ea" (/iː/) and start reading and spelling words that use it.

slides.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="320" height="320" role="img" aria-label="leaf" class="wp-icon wp-raster" data-picture="leaf"><image href="data:image/png;base64," x="0" y="0" width="100" height="100" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"/></svg>

slides.mnemonic: Minty Leaf grows on the tea bush, and when the wind blows through her she rustles out a long 'ea, ea' sound.

character.name: Minty Leaf
character.blurb: Minty Leaf is a fresh green leaf from the tea bush, and she whispers 'ea' whenever a breeze passes through the branches.

slides.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ee' in tree — 'ea' is very common in the middle of words.
slides.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'a', close together — two letters, one sound.
slides.action: Children mime picking a leaf and holding it near their lips, then blow gently while saying 'ea' in a long stretched-out breath.
slides.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="320" height="320" role="img" aria-label="leaf" class="wp-icon wp-raster" data-picture="leaf"><image href="data:image/png;base64," x="0" y="0" width="100" height="100" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"/></svg>

slides.tip: The 'ay' doesn't say its usual sound here — this word rhymes with 'fez', not with 'days', even though it's the family word for 'say'.

slides.heading: Tue
slides.objective: Learn the new sound "oy" (/ɔɪ/) and start reading and spelling words that use it.

slides.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-90 -110 180 180" width="320" height="320" role="img" aria-label="boy" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" class="wp-icon" data-picture="boy"><rect x="-24" y="-94" width="48" height="94" rx="14" ry="14" fill="#f6a8c0" stroke="#88283f" stroke-width="3.5"/><path d="M-22 -84q-14 8-14 26" fill="none" stroke="#88283f" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M22 -84q14 8 14 26" fill="none" stroke="#88283f" stroke-width="5"/><circle cx="0" cy="-116" r="28" fill="#deac71" stroke="#6f4318" stroke-width="3.5"/><path d="M-28 -116Q-28 -155.2 0 -155.2Q28 -155.2 28 -116Q15.4 -124.4 0 -123Q-15.4 -124.4 -28 -116Z" fill="#c99a63" stroke="#6d4318" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="6" cy="-118" r="9.35" fill="#1d2b38" stroke="none"/><circle cx="3.11" cy="-121.06" r="3.06" fill="#ffffff" stroke="none"/></svg>

slides.mnemonic: Joy Butterfly can't sit still — whenever she finds a new flower she loops in the air and calls out 'oy!' with delight.

character.name: Joy Butterfly
character.blurb: Joy Butterfly has bright coral wings dotted with spots, and she calls out 'oy' whenever something makes her happy, always at the end of her little song.

slides.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oi' in coin — 'oy' is usually used at the end of a word.
slides.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'y', close together — two letters, one sound.
slides.action: Children throw both arms up in a cheer and jump once, calling 'oy!' like they've just spotted a friend.

slides.dictation: A boy can enjoy a toy.

slides.heading: Wed
slides.objective: Learn the new sound "ir" (/ɜː/) and start reading and spelling words that use it.

slides.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="320" height="320" role="img" aria-label="bird" class="wp-icon wp-raster" data-picture="bird_pet"><image href="data:image/png;base64," x="0" y="0" width="100" height="100" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"/></svg>

slides.mnemonic: Twirl the Wren spins in a tight little circle on her branch and hums a low 'ir' as she turns.

character.name: Twirl the Wren
character.blurb: Twirl the Wren has one teal tuft on her head and loves to spin round and round on the spot, humming 'ir' the whole time.

slides.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ur' in burn — 'ir' often appears in the middle of a word, right inside the word 'bird' itself.
slides.formation_cue: Write 'i', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.
slides.action: Children put one finger up and spin slowly on the spot, humming 'ir' until they stop.
slides.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="320" height="320" role="img" aria-label="bird" class="wp-icon wp-raster" data-picture="bird_pet"><image href="data:image/png;base64," x="0" y="0" width="100" height="100" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"/></svg>

slides.heading: Thu
slides.objective: Extra practice blending and segmenting everything taught this week — no new content today.

slides.dictation: A ship is on the sea.

slides.heading: Fri
slides.objective: Revisit everything taught this week, read the matched decodable book, and check how securely it has been learned.

slides.dictation: A snail is on a leaf.
